analysis.one_liner: Allows cheap prescription drug imports and expands health coverage for children, pregnant women, and small businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 24, 2005 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada, Europe, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and Switzerland, with registration and inspection rules to keep out counterfeits. It would let states cover more children, pregnant women, and legal immigrants through Medicaid and the children's health insurance program, give small businesses a tax credit toward employee health insurance, and create a federal office to push hospitals and doctors toward shared electronic health records. It was introduced by Senator Edward Kennedy and 17 Democratic cosponsors and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay some of the highest brand-name drug prices in the world, uninsured low-income children and pregnant women whose states choose to expand Medicaid or CHIP coverage, legal immigrants eligible for optional coverage, small employers struggling to afford employee health insurance, and patients who would benefit from required drug-safety studies and standardized quality reporting. The bill's own findings estimate open drug markets could save consumers at least $38 billion a year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, uninsured families, and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the current ban and requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to write rules allowing importation of qualifying prescription drugs from registered exporters and pharmacies, with personal importation of up to a 90-day supply from Canada starting within months of enactment [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that Americans pay up to five times more to fill prescriptions than consumers in other countries and estimate that open pharmaceutical markets could save American consumers at least $38 billion each year [S3].

Gives states the option to expand Medicaid and SCHIP coverage to low-income children, pregnant women, and legal immigrants, removes the funding cap on SCHIP for states that expand child eligibility, and requires group insurers to offer dependent coverage to workers with children [S2] [S3].

Gives small businesses a refundable tax credit for a portion of employee health insurance costs and creates a new health insurance coverage title for small firms, plus 'three-share' programs splitting costs among workers, employers, and the state [S2] [S3].

Authorizes the Secretary to require post-approval safety studies when credible safety questions arise, and creates an Office of Health Information Technology plus uniform quality measures across Medicare, military, and veterans health programs [S2] [S3].

Adds antitrust rules making it unlawful for drug manufacturers to charge exporters higher prices, cut off supplies to importers, or make US-specific drug differences designed to block importation, with violations punishable by up to 10 years in prison for fraudulent notices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US prices would face competition from the same drugs sold cheaper abroad and who could no longer restrict supplies or differentiate products to block importation. Federal taxpayers would fund the small-business tax credits and the federal share of state Medicaid and SCHIP expansions, and the FDA would take on new registration, inspection, and recall duties financed by fees on registered importers and exporters capped at 1 percent of imported drug value.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Importation carries safety risks: the bill relies on registered exporters, chain-of-custody records, and FDA inspections to keep counterfeit or substandard drugs out, and it excludes biologics, controlled substances, and certain restricted drugs, but critics argued foreign supply chains could not be policed as tightly as domestic ones [S3].

The coverage expansions and small-business tax credits are largely optional for states and would add federal spending, and the bill pays for none of it with offsetting cuts or revenue; the CRS summary identifies no dedicated funding source beyond fees on drug importers [S2] [S3].
One provision would forfeit a family's personal income tax exemption for any child not covered by health insurance, effectively a new tax penalty on parents of uninsured children [S3].

Drug importation of the kind this bill authorizes was repeatedly enacted in later Congresses only on a pilot basis and was never implemented at scale, partly because of safety concerns and manufacturer resistance, so the promised savings were uncertain even on the bill's own terms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits are large and concrete: cheaper medicines for tens of millions of Americans and state options to insure more children and pregnant women. The bill tries hard to answer the safety objection with registration, inspection, and recall requirements, and funds oversight through fees on importers rather than general revenue. The honest cost side is real but modest: some fiscal exposure from the tax credits and state expansions with no offsets, a new penalty on parents of uninsured children, and residual counterfeit-drug risk that no regulatory scheme fully eliminates. On balance this is a consumer- and family-focused bill whose main obstacle was not design but the absence of any committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing or vote, until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Affordable Health Care Act on January 24, 2005, with Senators Reid, Stabenow, Corzine, Schumer, Mikulski, Akaka, Inouye, Levin, Kerry, Lautenberg, Rockefeller, Dodd, Pryor, and Durbin joining as original sponsors [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; that referral is the last action recorded for the bill in the 109th Congress [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee report, floor vote, or companion House action appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].
All 17 cosponsors were Democrats, in a Senate where Republicans held the majority and controlled the Finance Committee's schedule [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers were better off, because the bill's price competition and anti-blocking provisions never advanced; so were members of the majority who avoided a vote on drug importation. American consumers did not get the savings or coverage the bill proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and the majority

against.role: Industry whose US prices the importation title would expose to foreign competition
against.what_they_did: Opposed prescription drug importation legislation during this period, arguing it could not guarantee drug safety and would undermine pharmaceutical revenue

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 17 senators, all D — while Republicans held the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chair, and no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: The bill exposes their US prices to competition from the same drugs sold cheaper in Canada, Europe, Japan, and elsewhere, and bars them from cutting supplies to exporters or altering products to block importation. Consumers would pay less for identical medicines; the industry would lose the pricing power that comes from a closed US market.

industries.industry: Canadian and foreign internet pharmacies (registered exporters)
industries.note: The bill creates a legal, FDA-supervised export business for licensed foreign pharmacies shipping 90-day supplies to US patients, with Canadian exporters given priority registration. Their gain is consumers' savings, though their incentive is volume of US sales.

industries.industry: US pharmacies and drug wholesalers (as registered importers)
industries.note: Registered importers gain a new, legal channel to buy cheaper drugs abroad and resell at home, passing savings to patients, but they pay registration and inspection fees capped at 1 percent of import value and bear compliance burdens.

A new federal Office of Health Information Technology and uniform quality reporting across Medicare, military, and veterans programs would drive public and provider spending on electronic records systems. Better data could improve care quality, but vendors become the channel through which that modernization is purchased.
A refundable tax credit would cover part of employee health insurance costs, lowering a burden that falls on small firms and their workers alike.
